implementation_notes: The modern C++ realization of the Prototype pattern is the virtual constructor idiom: a pure virtual clone() in the base class calls each concrete class's copy constructor, so clients copy through Base&/Base* without knowing the dynamic type. Return std::unique_ptr<Base> (C++11) so ownership is explicit and no leak survives an exception; covariance is not available for smart pointers, so derived overrides keep the base return type. For plain value types skip clone() entirely and copy by value - the hierarchy is only justified when the copy must be polymorphic.
pitfalls: Slicing: Shape s = *ptr; copies only the base subobject - clones must be stored and passed as pointers or references to the base.
A clone() that returns by value, or a base class without a virtual destructor, silently loses the derived type or leaks on deletion.
std::unique_ptr<Base> is not covariant with std::unique_ptr<Derived>; overrides must keep the base return type (wrap a covariant raw-pointer helper instead of changing the return type).
A class with raw owning pointers gets its inherited copy constructor, so clone() copies the pointers; clone is a double-free unless the class follows the rule of three/five.

variants.name: Covariant clone() returning a raw pointer (classic)
variants.implementation_notes: Pre-C++11 form: clone() returns a raw pointer and derived classes narrow the return type to the concrete class - covariant return types were standardised in C++98 and let callers who already know the type avoid a cast. The caller owns the result and must delete it, so wrap the returned pointer in std::unique_ptr immediately at the call site. Choose this form only for legacy APIs or where the concrete return type is genuinely needed by the caller.
pitfalls: The caller-owned raw pointer leaks on early return or when the next statement throws; convert to a smart pointer immediately.
Covariance works only for raw pointers and references - smart pointer return types are unrelated types to the compiler.
A covariant clone() still needs the base to be copy-constructible and the derived classes to chain copy constructors correctly.

variants.name: CRTP Cloneable mixin injecting clone()
variants.implementation_notes: In wide hierarchies the one-line clone() has to be written in every class; a CRTP mixin writes it once and injects the correct derived type into each concrete class. It removes the copy-paste failure mode (a forgotten or mistyped clone) while keeping the same interface and the same smart-pointer return. The mixin requires C++11 for std::unique_ptr and demands that every derived class be copy-constructible.
pitfalls: The static_cast is safe only when D really is the most-derived type and the mixin is instantiated exactly once per class; diamond/virtual inheritance breaks that assumption.
The mixin hides the base constructors and assignment operators - add using B::B / using B::operator= or they disappear from the derived class.
Injecting clone() via a template means the class is no longer trivially copyable or standard-layout; do not use it where the type must stay POD.
